'''''Cota tinctoria''''', the '''golden marguerite''', '''yellow chamomile''', or '''oxeye chamomile''', is a [[species]] of [[perennial plant|perennial]] flowering plant in the [[Asteraceae|sunflower family]]. Other common names include '''dyer's chamomile''', '''Boston daisy''', and '''Paris daisy'''. In horticulture this plant is still widely referred to by its synonym '''''Anthemis tinctoria'''''.<ref>{{cite book|title=RHS A–Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

It is a short-lived plant often treated as [[biennial plant|biennial]], native to Europe, the Mediterranean and Western Asia and naturalized in scattered locations in North America.<ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=cota+tinctoria Altervista Flora Italiana,  Camomilla dei tintori, Färberkamille, ''Cota tinctoria'' (L.) J. Gay] includes many photos plus European distribution map</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Cota%20tinctoria.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref> It has aromatic, bright green, feathery foliage. The serrate leaves are bi-pinnatifid (= finely divided) and downy beneath. It grows to a height of {{convert|60|cm|in|abbr=on}}.<ref name=wilma/>

It has yellow daisy-like terminal [[flower head]]s on long thin angular stems, blooming in profusion during the summer.<ref name=wilma>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250066437 Flora of North America, Golden marguerite, yellow chamomile, ''Cota tinctoria'' (Linnaeus) J. Gay ex Gussone, Fl. Sicul. Syn. 2: 867. 1845. ]</ref>

It has no culinary or commercial uses and only limited medicinal uses. However, it produces excellent yellow, buff and golden-orange dyes, used in the past for fabrics.<ref>[http://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=7001555&PTRefFk=7000000 Euro+Med PlantBase - the information resource for Euro-Mediterranean plant diversity]</ref>

''Cota tinctoria'' is grown in gardens for its bright attractive flowers and fine lacy foliage; there is a white-flowering form. Under the synonym ''Anthemis tinctoria'', the [[cultivar]] 'E.C. Buxton' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/98124/i-Anthemis-tinctoria-i-E-c-Buxton/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Anthemis tinctoria'' 'E.C. Buxton'
| publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate=12 January 2018}}</ref> The popular seed-raised cultivar 'Kelwayi' has 5 cm wide, yellow flowers on 65 cm plants.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gardenia.net/plant/anthemis-tinctoria-kelwayii-golden-marguerite | title = ''Anthemis tinctoria'' 'Kelwayi' | website = Gardenia.net | access-date = 12 July 2021}}</ref>

The species hybridizes with ''[[Tripleurospermum inodorum]]'' to form the hybrid [[× Tripleurocota|× ''Tripleurocota sulfurea'']].<ref name=POWO_77081589-1>{{Cite POWO|title=''× Tripleurocota sulfurea'' (P.Fourn.) Starm..|id=77081589-1|access-date=2023-12-05|mode=cs1}}</ref>
